newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia asks rights body to prove riots report.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia asks rights body to prove riots report.

text.p: The Indonesian government said on Friday it was surprised by a national human rights commission report that five people died in riots in Jakarta in July and 74 were still missing, and called on it to prove the figures.
"The government had explained the July 27 events as they were. The government is surprised by the figures of dead and missing given by the rights commission," State Secretary Murdiono told reporters.
"Therefore, the goverment wants the rights commission to prove the figures with acceptable evidence," Murdiono said.
The government has said three people died and has made no mention of missing.
Murdiono added, however, that the government had no intention of intervening in the functioning of the commission.
Indonesia's official Human Rights Commission said last week it had confirmed that at least five people were killed in the July 27 riots, the worst violence in the capital for more than two decades.

Deputy chairman Marzuki Darusman and Secretary-General Baharuddin Lopa, issuing the preliminary findings of the body's fact-finding team, also said 74 people had been reported missing after the trouble.
Lopa told reporters the known deaths had been confirmed by doctors at Jakarta hospitals, but the commission did not have complete details about where and when the five died.

The riots started after police raided the office of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) in central Jakarta. The office was occupied by loyalist supporters of the ousted party leader Megawati Sukarnoputri.
Megawati loyalist Kwik Kian Gie said in a statement on Friday that her faction of the PDI would open a new office in East Jakarta on Monday.
Megawati, daughter of late founding president Sukarno, was replaced in June by deputy parliament speaker Surjadi at a government-backed congress of party rebels in Medan, North Sumatra.
Megawati said in a statement issued on Friday to mark the end of the traditional 40-day mouring period since July 27 that her party executive board had noted the commission's figure of 74 missing.
"We still do not know where they are. It is also not known which among them have died," she said.
After the human rights commission's report, an Indonesian army official said the government had no intention of investigating the reported disappearances.

General Syarwan Hamid, chief of the army's socio-political affairs unit, was quoted in the Republika daily newspaper on Monday as saying that the figure of 74 missing was not a serious issue and that the people had "simply just not gone home."
The commission also said 149 people, including security officials, were injured during the disturbances.
